title: Tomatoes at $6, Rice Up 15 Per Cent: Inside the Grocery Squeeze Hitting NRI Households Hardest
excerpt: A toxic mix of fuel surcharges, tariffs, and the Iran conflict has pushed American food prices to a three-year high — and South Asian staples are disproportionately affected
body:
For Meera Krishnamurthy, a software engineer in Fremont, California, the inflation crisis became personal at the Indian grocery store. The five-kilogram bag of basmati rice she buys fortnightly had gone from $12 to nearly $14 in two months. Toor dal was up 20 per cent. Even the humble tomato — indispensable in any South Indian kitchen — was selling at prices that would have scandalised her mother in Chennai.

Krishnamurthy's experience is not anecdotal. It is statistical. American grocery prices rose 0.7 per cent in April alone, the steepest monthly increase since the government shutdown of late 2025. Year-over-year, food prices have climbed 2.9 per cent, with fresh vegetables leading the surge at a startling 6.1 per cent. Tomatoes, which travel long distances from farms in Mexico and Florida, have jumped 40 per cent over the past 12 months.

## The triple squeeze

Three forces have converged to create what economists are calling a "perfect inflationary storm." The first is energy. The ongoing conflict between the United States and Iran, which has disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, has pushed gasoline prices above $4.50 per gallon and diesel to nearly $5.70. Since virtually every item in an American grocery store arrives by truck, the fuel surcharge cascades through the entire supply chain. Distributors report paying up to 50 per cent more to transport fresh produce.

The second force is tariffs. The Trump administration's levies on imports from China, Mexico, and Canada have added costs to everything from canned goods to fertiliser. Steel tariffs have raised the price of tin cans, making staples like canned beans and corn more expensive. Analysts estimate that produce prices could rise by 25 per cent if the tariffs on Mexican imports remain in place through the summer.

The third is fertiliser. Nitrogen fertiliser prices have surged 30 per cent since February, with urea up 47 per cent, according to the American Farm Bureau Federation. This will feed directly into the cost of domestically grown crops later this year, creating a delayed but durable wave of inflation.

## Why South Asian households feel it more

The standard American inflation narrative focuses on generic grocery baskets. But for Indian, Pakistani, and Bangladeshi households in the United States — a demographic that now numbers over five million — the pain is concentrated in specific categories. Basmati rice, lentils, fresh vegetables, and cooking oils are staples, not luxuries. Many of these items are imported or grown in small quantities domestically, making them more sensitive to supply-chain disruptions.

Ethnic grocery stores, which operate on thinner margins than major supermarket chains, have less capacity to absorb price increases. A survey by the Asian American Grocers Association found that South Asian grocery retailers have raised prices by an average of 8 per cent since January, compared with 3 per cent at mainstream supermarkets.

The broader consumer price index, which rose to 3.8 per cent in April — a three-year high — tells only part of the story. For households that spend a larger share of income on food (as lower- and middle-income immigrant families typically do), the effective inflation rate is considerably higher.

## No relief in sight

Economists warn that the worst may not be over. If the Strait of Hormuz remains partially blocked through the summer, energy costs will continue to ripple through the food chain. A Senate hearing on supply-chain resilience heard testimony that grocery prices could spike further by July.

For the Indian diaspora, the squeeze arrives at an awkward moment. Remittances to India — which hit a record $125 billion in 2025 — depend on disposable income that is now being eroded. Families that have historically sent money home for weddings, education, and medical expenses are being forced to recalculate.

The inflationary storm will pass eventually. But its lesson will linger: even in the world's wealthiest country, the distance between comfort and strain can be measured in the price of a bag of rice.
